hypothesis: Replacing the 4x-unrolled byte reject inside the string-skip loop of LineIndex.build (src/indexer/lineIndex.ts L256-282 on 1d2377e) with an aligned Uint32Array SWAR word loop that tests each 4-byte word for a 0x22 or 0x5c lane via the haszero trick ((v - 0x01010101) & ~v & 0x80808080 on v = x ^ 0x22222222 and v = x ^ 0x5c5c5c5c), with the existing byte path kept as the unaligned head/tail and hit-word fallback, will raise the primary speedup from 1.623 to ~1.83 (~1.13x relative), because it checks 4 string bytes per typed-array load with one combined branch instead of 4 loads and 4 compares, and it never stops on in-string bytes <= 0x5c other than quote/backslash. This stacks on the merged round-2 string loop and round-3 WCLS outer skip. This is the only change: the escaped-carry branch, the outside-string switch, checkpoint modulo, record pushes, for-await loop, Buffer.from conversion and EOF handling are untouched.

steps.change: At the start of each chunk iteration (after `const buf = Buffer.isBuffer(raw) ? raw : Buffer.from(raw);` around L247), add per-chunk Uint32Array view setup with alignment calculation: `const base = buf.byteOffset; const aOff = (base + 3) & ~3; const wN = base + n > aOff ? (base + n - aOff) >> 2 : 0; const u32 = new Uint32Array(buf.buffer, aOff, wN);`. This creates an aligned word view starting at the first 4-byte boundary at or after buf's base, with length in words covering the chunk's byte range. For unaligned or short chunks wN will be 0 and the word loop will be skipped.

Inside the string-skip loop (currently L256-282, the `while (inString && i < n)` block), replace the existing 4x-unrolled byte reject (`while (i + 3 < n) { if (buf[i] <= 0x5c || buf[i+1] <= 0x5c || buf[i+2] <= 0x5c || buf[i+3] <= 0x5c) break; i += 4; }`) with an alignment-gated word loop: `if (((base + i) & 3) === 0) { let w = (base + i - aOff) >> 2; while (w < wN) { const x = u32[w]; const a = x ^ 0x22222222, c = x ^ 0x5c5c5c5c; if (((((a - 0x01010101) & ~a) | ((c - 0x01010101) & ~c)) & 0x80808080) !== 0) break; w++; } i = aOff - base + (w << 2); }`. This checks alignment first, then walks words testing for 0x22 or 0x5c in any lane via haszero, updating i to the byte position after the last clean word. The alignment guard ensures the word loop only runs when i is at a word boundary; otherwise the existing byte tail handles it.

Keep the existing byte tail (`while (i < n) { const b = buf[i]; if (b === 0x22) { inString = false; lineHasContent = true; i++; break; } if (b === 0x5c) { escaped = true; i++; if (i < n) i++; break; } i++; }`) unchanged. This handles the unaligned head (before alignment is reached), the tail (after the last full word), and the hit-word fallback (when haszero detects a quote or backslash). The byte tail naturally advances i to the next aligned boundary if it starts unaligned, so unaligned subarrays, pooled Buffer.from(string) buffers, and 1-byte splits will pass.

Leave the escaped-carry logic (the `if (escaped) { escaped = false; if (i < n) i++; }` block at the top of the string loop), the outside-string switch statement, the checkpoint modulo logic (`if (lineHasContent && o % cpInterval === 0)`), the record pushes (`offsets.push(o); lines.push(line);`), the for-await chunk loop (`for await (const raw of handle)`), the Buffer.from conversion, and the EOF record handling all untouched. Only the string-skip inner loop body changes; everything else stays identical to the current merged code (1d2377e).

expected_outcome.rationale: Scratch measurements on the same merged baseline (1d2377e: round-2 string loop + round-3 WCLS outer skip) showed relative speedup of 1.144 / 1.113 / 1.116 / 1.168 across 4 passes (median ~1.13x) when swarU32 was tested alone. Expected sealed score is 1.623 × 1.13 ≈ 1.83, crossing the harness target of 1.8. The haszero trick tests 4 bytes per load with one combined branch instead of 4 separate compares, and it only stops on the exact two bytes (0x22, 0x5c) that change state, so it stays fast on real-world strings with spaces/digits/punctuation where the byte reject would drop to the tail. Correctness was confirmed on all sealed edge fixtures (whole/1/2/7/64/1000-byte splits, intervals 1024/1/3, async-iterable and string chunks, plus extras: trailing backslash at EOF, escaped-quote runs, unicode/emoji, leading empty lines, raw newlines inside strings). The haszero formula is byte-wise so endianness does not matter, and a false positive only causes an early drop to the byte path (correctness preserved).

history_reference.builds_on: round_2_planner_a (string-skip loop with 4x byte reject, winner score 1.499) and round_3_planner_a (WCLS outer skip, winner score 1.623). This change replaces the byte reject with a word-level SWAR test, stacking on both merged wins.
history_reference.avoids: round_3_planner_b (swarU32 alone tested before the outer skip was merged, score 1.587). That plan was correct but ranked below the outer skip. Now that the outer skip is merged, this plan tests swarU32 stacked on top of both prior wins, which the round-3 brief predicted would reach ~1.80-1.85 sealed. Also avoids round_2_planner_b (outer skip tested alone on the baseline, score 0.869, failed because 75% of bytes were inside strings) and round_2_planner_c (sync array iteration, score 0.882, no effect because per-byte work dominates).
